Disprove a universal claim by exhibiting a single case where it fails. One counterexample suffices.
Base case + inductive step (assume true for n = k, prove for n = k + 1). Used for sums, divisibility, inequalities.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Proof — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Proof brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Proof.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which proof technique is best for disproving 'all primes are odd'?
options: counterexample
induction
contradiction
direct proof

mcqs.q: Induction is most suited for statements about:
options: positive integers
real numbers in general
complex numbers only
irrational numbers
Eventually a term will be so small it equals 0.
No — it approaches 0 as the limit but no term is ever exactly 0.
It reaches 0 at the millionth term.
They are perpendicular.

mcqs.q: Does the limit of f(x) as x approaches a have to equal f(a)?
options: Limits always equal zero unless the function is constant.
The limit is always just the value of f at that point — that's how you compute it.
They are perpendicular.
No — the limit can exist even if f(a) is undefined or different from the limit.

mcqs.q: If two lines have the same gradient, what is true about them?
options: They are perpendicular.
It reaches 0 at the millionth term.
They are parallel (or the same line if their intercepts are also equal).
They cross each other at the y-intercept.
